modules.title: Foundation Building
modules.description: Perpetual futures fundamentals, mathematics of trading, architecture types, and opening your first position

questions.question: What is the key difference between perpetual futures and traditional futures?

options.text: Perpetuals have higher fees than traditional futures
Perpetuals have no expiration date and use funding rates to keep prices aligned with spot
Perpetuals can only be traded on centralized exchanges
Traditional futures offer more leverage than perpetuals

questions.explanation: Perpetual futures eliminate expiration dates by using a funding rate mechanism to keep the perpetual price aligned with the spot price, allowing positions to be held indefinitely.

questions.question: When the funding rate is positive, what happens?

options.text: Both sides receive payment from the protocol

questions.explanation: Positive funding occurs when perpetual price > spot price. Long positions pay short positions, which discourages buying and encourages selling, driving the perpetual price down toward spot.

questions.question: With 10x leverage and $1,000 margin, what is your position size?
questions.explanation: Position Size = Margin × Leverage. With $1,000 margin and 10x leverage, your position size is $1,000 × 10 = $10,000.

questions.question: What is the main difference between CLOB and Oracle-Based pool architectures?

options.text: CLOB uses market makers and order books; Oracle pools execute trades at oracle prices with zero slippage
Oracle pools are faster than CLOB exchanges
CLOB has zero slippage while Oracle pools have high slippage
There is no meaningful difference between them

questions.explanation: CLOB (Central Limit Order Book) uses market makers posting orders for price discovery with potential slippage. Oracle pools trade against a liquidity pool at oracle prices, offering zero price impact.

questions.question: What does the funding rate formula calculate?

options.text: The total fees paid to the exchange
The difference between perpetual price and spot price, determining payments between longs and shorts
The liquidation price of a position

questions.explanation: Funding Rate = (Perpetual Price - Spot Price) / Spot Price × Adjustment Factor. This determines whether longs pay shorts (positive) or shorts pay longs (negative).

questions.question: If hourly funding rate is 0.01%, what is the annualized rate?
questions.explanation: Annualized Rate = Hourly Rate × 24 hours × 365 days = 0.01% × 24 × 365 = 87.6% APR. High funding rates can significantly erode capital.

questions.question: What is the liquidation price for a long ETH position at $2,500 entry with 10x leverage?
questions.explanation: Liquidation occurs slightly before the theoretical 10% drop due to maintenance margin requirements. With 10x leverage, liquidation typically happens around 9-9.5% below entry, not exactly 10%.

questions.question: Which protocols use the Central Limit Order Book (CLOB) model?
questions.explanation: Hyperliquid, dYdX v4, and EdgeX all use CLOB architecture where market makers post orders and price discovery happens through supply and demand on the order book.

questions.question: What is the difference between initial margin and maintenance margin?

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
Initial margin is required to open; maintenance margin is the minimum to keep the position open
Initial margin is for shorts; maintenance margin is for longs
Initial margin is paid to the protocol; maintenance margin is paid to liquidity providers

questions.explanation: Initial margin is the collateral required to open a position (e.g., 10% for 10x leverage). Maintenance margin is the minimum required to keep the position open (e.g., 5%). Falling below maintenance triggers liquidation.

questions.question: Which margin mode should beginners use for their first trades?

options.text: Isolated margin to limit risk to only that position
It doesn't matter which mode you use

questions.explanation: Isolated margin limits your risk to only the margin allocated to that specific position. With cross margin, one bad trade can liquidate your entire account. Beginners should always use isolated margin.

questions.question: What is the recommended leverage range for beginner traders?
questions.explanation: Beginners should use 3x-5x leverage maximum. With 5x leverage, a 20% price move causes liquidation. Higher leverage dramatically increases liquidation risk.

questions.question: What is the key risk of oracle-based liquidity pools?

options.text: Oracle latency allowing arbitrage exploitation and pool insolvency risk

questions.explanation: Oracle-based pools face oracle latency risk (stale prices can be exploited by arbitrageurs) and pool insolvency risk (if traders consistently win, the pool can be drained).

questions.question: For a $10,000 position with 5x leverage, 0.05% trading fee, and $24 daily funding cost, what price movement do you need to break even after 24 hours?
questions.explanation: Break-even = (Fees + Funding) / Position Size = ($5 + $24) / $10,000 = 0.29%. You need at least 0.29% price movement just to cover costs.

questions.question: What is the recommended safety buffer between current price and liquidation price?
questions.explanation: A 20-30% safety buffer between current price and liquidation price helps avoid liquidation from normal market volatility. This provides room for price fluctuations.

questions.question: What should you always set before opening any position?

options.text: A stop loss order to limit maximum loss

questions.explanation: Always set a stop loss before opening any position. Stop losses limit your maximum loss, prevent emotional decisions, and protect your capital from unexpected market moves.

modules.title: Protocol Mastery
modules.description: Deep dive into Hyperliquid, GMX V2, Drift Protocol, and alternative chain protocols

questions.question: What is unique about Hyperliquid's HyperBFT consensus mechanism?

options.text: It uses proof of work like Bitcoin
It uses pipelined consensus allowing parallel block processing for sub-second latency
It cannot process more than 100 orders per second

questions.explanation: HyperBFT uses pipelined consensus derived from HotStuff protocol, allowing parallel processing of blocks. This enables ~200,000 orders/second and 0.2s median latency.

questions.question: How does Hyperliquid's zero-gas trading model work?

options.text: The protocol pays all gas fees
Users pay zero gas for placing/canceling orders; only trading fees on execution
Users must stake HYPE to get gas refunds
Gas is subsidized by token emissions

questions.explanation: Hyperliquid users pay zero gas for placing, canceling, or modifying orders. They only pay trading fees (maker/taker) upon successful execution, enabling high-frequency trading strategies.

questions.question: What is the HLP (Hyperliquidity Provider) vault?

options.text: A lending pool for borrowing USDC
A unified liquidity pool that acts as automated market maker and liquidation backstop

questions.explanation: The HLP vault is Hyperliquid's unified liquidity pool that algorithmically provides liquidity on the CLOB, serves as liquidation backstop, and allows retail to participate in market making.

questions.question: What key innovation did GMX V2 introduce compared to V1?

options.text: Isolated GM pools instead of unified GLP, enabling risk isolation
Lower trading fees across all markets

questions.explanation: GMX V2 moved from a unified GLP pool to isolated GM pools (GM-ETH-USDC, GM-BTC-USDC, etc.), providing risk isolation so one market's failure doesn't affect others.

questions.question: How does GMX V2's Chainlink Data Streams work?

options.text: Chainlink pushes prices every block automatically
Prices are pulled on-chain when trades occur, using keeper networks
GMX calculates prices using on-chain AMM formulas
Traders must manually submit price feeds

questions.explanation: GMX V2 uses a pull model where Chainlink aggregates prices off-chain, and keepers fetch the latest price signature when trades occur. This reduces oracle latency compared to push models.

questions.question: What are Drift Protocol's three layers of liquidity?

options.text: JIT (Just-In-Time) Auction, DLOB (Decentralized Limit Order Book), and DAMM (Dynamic AMM)

questions.explanation: Drift uses a three-layer liquidity trifecta: JIT auction (market makers compete to fill orders), DLOB (off-chain matching with on-chain settlement), and DAMM (dynamic AMM backstop).

questions.question: How does Drift's JIT auction protect LPs and improve trader execution?

options.text: By charging higher fees to market makers
Market makers compete in 5-second auctions to fill orders at better prices than AMM

questions.explanation: JIT auctions run for 5 seconds where market makers compete to fill orders at better prices than the AMM. This internalizes MEV for trader benefit and protects LPs from toxic flow.

questions.question: What is the key feature of Drift's cross-margin system?

options.text: Unified margin across spot, perps, lending, and prediction markets
Only USDC can be used as margin

questions.explanation: Drift's cross-margin system integrates spot trading, perpetual swaps, money markets, and prediction markets, all sharing the same collateral pool for maximum capital efficiency.

questions.question: What is the difference between standard and synthetic markets in GMX V2?

options.text: Standard has higher leverage; synthetic has lower leverage
Standard pools hold the actual traded tokens; synthetic pools use different backing (e.g., ETH backing DOGE market)
Standard is for BTC only; synthetic is for altcoins

questions.explanation: Standard markets (ETH/USD) hold the actual tokens being traded. Synthetic markets (DOGE/USD) use different backing like ETH+USDC, creating delta mismatch risk but enabling more asset listings.

questions.question: What makes EdgeX unique among perpetual DEXs?

options.text: It's the only DEX on Ethereum mainnet
Native iOS and Android mobile apps with hardware acceleration and persistent connections
It offers 1000x leverage on all pairs
It uses proof of stake consensus

questions.explanation: EdgeX offers native mobile apps (iOS/Android) with persistent WebSocket connections, GPU-accelerated charting, biometric security, and push notifications for mobile-first trading.

questions.question: How does Extended (formerly X10) solve the bridging problem for Starknet?

options.text: By requiring users to hold STRK tokens
Account abstraction allows EVM wallets to trade on Starknet without explicit bridging
By operating only on Ethereum mainnet

questions.explanation: Extended uses account abstraction to deploy Starknet smart contract wallets that accept Ethereum signatures. Users can trade on Starknet using MetaMask without explicit bridging or STRK tokens.

questions.question: What yield-bearing assets can be used as collateral on Extended?

options.text: stETH (Lido liquid staking) and sDAI (Maker yield-bearing stablecoin)

questions.explanation: Extended supports yield-bearing collateral including stETH (Lido) and sDAI (Maker). This allows traders to earn yield (~4-5% APR) on their collateral while trading.

questions.question: What is Jupiter's JLP pool?

options.text: A peer-to-pool liquidity index serving as counterparty to all trades

questions.explanation: Jupiter's JLP (Jupiter Liquidity Provider) is a unified pool containing SOL, ETH, WBTC, and stablecoins that serves as counterparty to all perpetual trades on the platform.

questions.question: What is the primary trust point (risk) when using Hyperliquid?

options.text: The bridge from Arbitrum to Hyperliquid L1 is a multisig wallet

questions.explanation: Hyperliquid's primary trust point is the bridge contract on Arbitrum, which is a multisig wallet. If signers collude or are compromised, bridged funds could be at risk.

questions.question: Which architecture is best for executing large orders with zero slippage?

options.text: Oracle-based shared liquidity pools like GMX

questions.explanation: Oracle-based pools like GMX execute trades at the oracle price with zero price impact, regardless of size (up to pool depth). CLOB exchanges have slippage on large orders that move the order book.

modules.title: Advanced Strategies
modules.description: Funding rate arbitrage, risk management, advanced topics, and building professional trading systems

questions.question: What is delta-neutral yield farming?

options.text: Long spot + Short perpetual to capture funding rates without price exposure
Trading only during low volatility periods
Providing liquidity on both sides of an AMM

questions.explanation: Delta-neutral yield farming involves buying spot asset and shorting an equal perpetual position. Net price exposure is ~0 (delta neutral), but you earn funding payments when rates are positive.

questions.question: What is basis in cash and carry arbitrage?

options.text: The difference between perpetual price and spot price

questions.explanation: Basis is the difference between perpetual price and spot price. When perp > spot, you can short perp and buy spot to capture the basis spread plus ongoing funding payments.

questions.question: What is the main risk of delta-neutral funding arbitrage?

options.text: Funding rate flipping from positive to negative, causing you to pay instead of receive

questions.explanation: The main risk is funding rate volatility. If rates flip from positive (you receive) to negative (you pay), your previously profitable position starts losing money.

questions.question: Cross-protocol arbitrage captures profit from what?

options.text: Different funding rates between protocols (long low-rate, short high-rate)

questions.explanation: Cross-protocol arbitrage exploits funding rate differentials. Go long on Protocol A (paying lower rate) and short on Protocol B (receiving higher rate) to capture the spread.

questions.question: Why is 0.01% hourly funding rate (87.6% APR) considered expensive?

options.text: On leveraged positions, funding is calculated on notional size, eroding margin rapidly
The rate only applies to large traders

questions.explanation: Funding is calculated on notional position size, not margin. With 10x leverage on $1,000 margin ($10,000 position), 87.6% APR means potentially losing your entire margin to funding alone.

questions.question: What is cross-margin contagion risk?

options.text: Positions on different exchanges affecting each other
One bad position draining your entire cross-margin account, liquidating all positions

questions.explanation: With cross-margin, all positions share the same collateral. If one position loses heavily, it can drain the entire account equity and trigger liquidation of all positions, not just the losing one.

questions.question: What is the 1-5% rule in position sizing?

options.text: Risk only 1-5% of total capital per trade to prevent single trades from destroying your account

questions.explanation: The 1-5% rule means risking only 1-5% of your total capital on any single trade. For $10,000 capital, max risk per trade would be $200-500, preventing catastrophic losses.

questions.question: What should you check before opening any perpetual position?

options.text: Funding rate, liquidation price, safety buffer, position size, and stop loss

questions.explanation: A complete pre-trade checklist includes: funding rate (check annualized cost), liquidation price, 20-30% safety buffer, appropriate position size (1-5% risk), and stop loss placement.

questions.question: What is the OI to Volume ratio used to detect?

options.text: Wash trading (high volume, tiny OI = potential manipulation)

questions.explanation: OI (Open Interest) to Volume ratio helps detect wash trading. Healthy markets have balanced OI and volume. High volume with tiny OI is a red flag for potential manipulation.

questions.question: What is MEV internalization in protocols like Drift?

options.text: JIT auctions force arbitrageurs to fill orders at better prices, benefiting traders instead of extracting value
Hiding order flow from the public
Charging higher fees for larger orders

questions.explanation: MEV internalization through JIT auctions forces arbitrageurs to compete to fill orders at better prices than the AMM. This converts MEV extraction into price improvement for traders.

questions.question: What advantage do yield-bearing collateral assets provide?

options.text: Earning staking/DSR yield on collateral, reducing net funding costs

questions.explanation: Yield-bearing collateral (stETH, sDAI) earns yield while being used as margin. If funding rate is 10% APR and collateral yields 4% APR, net cost is only 6% APR.

questions.question: What is a due diligence minimum score threshold before using a protocol?
questions.explanation: A professional due diligence framework should require at least 7/10 score across security, economics, technical, and community factors before using a protocol for trading.

questions.question: What is the recommended maximum total portfolio risk?
questions.explanation: Maximum portfolio risk should be kept below 10% of total capital. This means even if all positions go wrong simultaneously, you won't lose more than 10% of your trading capital.

questions.question: What are oracle-pegged orders?

options.text: Orders that float at a fixed offset from the oracle price (e.g., 'Oracle - $0.50')
Market orders executed at best price
Orders that are always filled first

questions.explanation: Oracle-pegged orders automatically adjust relative to oracle price. An order set at 'Oracle - $0.50' will float below the oracle price, eliminating the need to constantly cancel and replace orders.

questions.question: What distinguishes professional traders from the 70-90% who lose money?

options.text: Systematic frameworks including due diligence, risk management, and continuous improvement

questions.explanation: Professional traders use systematic frameworks: due diligence protocols, risk management rules, position sizing formulas, monitoring procedures, performance tracking, and continuous improvement processes.
